newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo July department store sales fall 5.7% yr/yr. [CORRECTED 06:12 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Tokyo July department store sales fall 5.7% yr/yr. [CORRECTED 06:12 GMT]

text.p: Sales at Tokyo department stores slipped 5.7 percent in July compared with a year earlier to 231.6 billion yen (corrects from 131.6 billion yen), the Japan Department Stores Association said on Friday.

Department store sales in the Tokyo area have been lower on a year-on-year basis since November 1996, except for March 1997, when sales surged ahead of a rise in the consumption tax to five percent from three percent in April.
Analysts said they expect department store sales to remain slow for at least a few more months as consumer spending remains sluggish.

"Sales will not recover during this business year due to (negative) effects caused by the cancellation of a special tax reduction in June and an increase in individual medical costs scheduled to take effect in September," said Kazutoshi Aratake, an economist at Nikko Research Center.
The dampening effects of the consumption tax rise should have subsided by now, he added.
Futoshi Saito, an industry analyst at Daiwa Institute of Research, said department store sales would stay slow for a few more months but pick up after October depending on the weather.
Sales were down on a year-on-year basis for a fourth consecutive month due to sluggish bargain sales and slow demand in the mid-year gift-giving season, the association said.
It attributed the fall to the lingering effects of the consumption tax increase.
Individual consumer demand showed a feeble recovery compared to the previous month, but corporate demand remained low, it added.
The survey covered 31 outlets of 15 department stores in the Tokyo area.
Among items which performed better were men and women's clothing, sales of which increased slightly from the previous month helped by clearance sales.
July clothing sales fell 2.7 percent from the previous year, compared to a 6.5 percent year-on-year decline in June.

Sales of household items such as furniture and electrical appliances were still affected by the rise in consumption tax in April, and fell 16.5 percent compared with a year earlier, the association said.
